lead: Prestressed concrete is concrete squeezed on purpose before it carries load. A stretched high-strength steel tendon puts it into compression, and the bending from the load must use up that stored compression before tension can appear, so cracks come much later or never. The same idea lets a beam be shallower and span farther than reinforced concrete: bridge girders, metro viaduct segments, railway sleepers, poles, water tanks and hollow-core slabs.
prereq: You need the properties of concrete and reinforcing steel (characteristic strength, modulus of elasticity) and the bending stress f = My/I from limit state design of beams.

blocks.text: Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension. Its flexural tensile strength, the modulus of rupture, is only fcr = 0.7√fck by IS 456: about 4.4 N/mm² for M40 concrete against a cube strength of 40 N/mm². Reinforced concrete accepts this: the concrete cracks and bars carry the tension.
Prestressing changes the order: the concrete is compressed first, and the load must cancel that compression before it can cause tension.

The force comes from a tendon, a high-tensile steel wire, strand or bar stretched by a hydraulic jack. The jacking force P0 is the tendon force while the jack holds it. Transfer is the moment that force is handed to the concrete. In a pre-tensioned member the tendon is cut or released from its bed and grips the concrete by bond; in a post-tensioned member the jack is removed and the tendon bears on the concrete through end anchorages. The force left in the tendon later is smaller than P0 because of losses of prestress.

The eccentricity e is the distance from the centroidal axis of the concrete section to the tendon, in mm. A concentric tendon (e = 0) gives the same compression P/A at every fibre. A tendon below the axis also bends the section upward with a prestress moment P × e, adding compression at the bottom, where the load will cause tension.

At any fibre the stress is the sum of three parts: the axial squeeze P/A, the bending P·e/Z caused by the eccentric tendon, and the bending M/Z from the load. In this unit compression is positive and tension negative. For the top and bottom fibres of a rectangular section, Z = bD²/6:

f<sub>top</sub> = P/A − P·e/Z + M/Z
f<sub>bottom</sub> = P/A + P·e/Z − M/Z
blocks.where: f is the fibre stress in N/mm² (compression positive); P is the tendon force in N; A is the concrete area in mm²; e is the eccentricity below the centroid in mm; Z = I/y is the section modulus in mm³ for that fibre; M is the sagging moment from the load in N·mm. The signs above hold for a tendon below the centroid and a sagging moment.

blocks.text: As load grows, the bottom stress falls. The moment that brings the bottom stress exactly to zero is the decompression moment. Beyond it the bottom goes into tension, and it cracks when that tension reaches fcr. The upward bending P × e also gives a prestressed beam a small upward camber before load. Making a curved tendon's upward push cancel part of the load is load balancing.

items: The section stays uncracked, or has only fine cracks, at service load: good for durability, water tanks, pipes and members in coastal air.
Smaller and lighter sections for the same span, so less dead load on columns and foundations; long spans become practical.
High-strength steel and concrete are used at high stresses, so less material carries the same load.
Deflection is small because the section is uncracked and the camber offsets part of the sag.
Better shear and fatigue resistance: the compression reduces diagonal tension and the steel stress changes little under repeated load.

blocks.text: The cost is skill and hardware: jacks, anchorages, ducts, grout, strong concrete and supervision. The large force entering at a small anchorage needs its own steel in the anchorage zone. For short spans and light loads, ordinary reinforced concrete is usually cheaper. The method was made practical by Eugène Freyssinet in France around 1928, once high-tensile steel was available to survive the long-term losses.

examples.question: A rectangular beam 200 mm wide and 400 mm deep carries a straight tendon with force P = 400 kN. (a) Find the stresses when the tendon is concentric. (b) Find the top and bottom stresses when the tendon is 100 mm below the centroid. (c) A sagging moment of 56 kN·m is then applied. Find the top and bottom stresses for both tendon positions, and say which beam cracks if the concrete is M40. (d) Find the moment that brings the bottom stress to zero in each case.
steps: (a) Concentric: P/A = 400,000/80,000 = 5 N/mm² compression at every fibre.
(b) Prestress bending: P·e/Z = 400,000 × 100/(5.333 × 10⁶) = 7.5 N/mm². Top = 5 − 7.5 = −2.5 N/mm², that is 2.5 N/mm² tension; bottom = 5 + 7.5 = 12.5 N/mm² compression.
(c) Load bending: M/Z = 56 × 10⁶/(5.333 × 10⁶) = 10.5 N/mm², compression at the top and tension at the bottom.
Eccentric tendon: top = −2.5 + 10.5 = 8 N/mm² compression; bottom = 12.5 − 10.5 = 2 N/mm² compression. No tension anywhere.
Concentric tendon: top = 5 + 10.5 = 15.5 N/mm²; bottom = 5 − 10.5 = −5.5 N/mm², that is 5.5 N/mm² tension.
Cracking check: f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√40 = 4.43 N/mm². The concentric beam's bottom tension 5.5 N/mm² exceeds it, so that beam cracks; the eccentric beam is still in compression.
(d) Bottom stress zero when M/Z equals the bottom prestress: eccentric M = 12.5 × 5.333 × 10⁶ = 66.7 kN·m; concentric M = 5 × 5.333 × 10⁶ = 26.7 kN·m.
examples.answer: Concentric: 5 N/mm² everywhere. Eccentric: 2.5 N/mm² tension at the top and 12.5 N/mm² compression at the bottom before load; under 56 kN·m it has 8 N/mm² (top) and 2 N/mm² (bottom), both compression, while the concentric beam has 5.5 N/mm² bottom tension and cracks. The same 400 kN placed 100 mm low lifts the zero-tension moment from 26.7 to 66.7 kN·m, 2.5 times.

traps: Prestress does not make concrete strong in tension. It only stores compression; if the load's tension exceeds that compression plus f<sub>cr</sub>, the section still cracks.

Sign slips. Keep compression positive all the way. A tendon below the axis gives tension at the top before load (2.5 N/mm² in the worked example), and that top tension at transfer is a real check, not a rounding error.
Eccentricity is measured from the centroid of the concrete section, never from the top or bottom face.
The jacking force is not the force that stays. Use the force after losses for the service check.

quiz.q: Define tendon, jacking force and transfer.
quiz.a: A tendon is a high-tensile steel wire, strand or bar that carries the prestressing force. The jacking force is the tendon force while the jack holds it. Transfer is the handing of that force to the concrete: by bond in pre-tensioning, through end anchorages in post-tensioning.

quiz.q: State four advantages of prestressed concrete over reinforced concrete.
quiz.a: Uncracked or finely cracked section at service; smaller, lighter sections and longer spans; efficient use of high-strength materials; small deflection; better shear and fatigue resistance.

quiz.q: Why does a prestressed beam stay uncracked at a load where a similar reinforced concrete beam has already cracked?
quiz.a: The tendon has already put the concrete into compression. The load must first cancel that compression (decompression) and then exceed the modulus of rupture before a crack forms. In reinforced concrete the steel is passive, so the concrete takes the tension from the start.

quiz.q: Why is the tendon placed below the centroid in a simply supported beam?
quiz.a: The load causes tension at the bottom. A low tendon adds the moment P × e, which puts extra compression exactly where the load will cause tension, so a larger load is needed to reach zero stress there.

quiz.q: A 150 mm × 300 mm section carries a concentric tendon force of 300 kN. Find the stress.
quiz.a: A = 45,000 mm². P/A = 300,000/45,000 = 6.67 N/mm² compression, uniform over the section.

quiz.q: The same 300 kN tendon is moved 75 mm below the centroid of the 150 mm × 300 mm section. Find the top and bottom stresses before load.
In the worked example, the designer wants zero tension at the top before load. Find the largest eccentricity allowed and comment on the zero-tension moment at the bottom.
quiz.a: Top = P/A − P·e/Z = 0 gives e = Z/A = 5.333 × 10⁶/80,000 = 66.7 mm (the kern distance, D/6). Bottom prestress is then 2 × 5 = 10 N/mm², so the bottom reaches zero at M = 10 × 5.333 × 10⁶ = 53.3 kN·m, less than the 66.7 kN·m with e = 100 mm. Removing all top tension costs capacity; the self-weight acting at transfer usually allows a larger e.

beyond: Not for the exam. Many new bridges use external tendons, placed outside the concrete inside the box girder, so they can be inspected and replaced. Unbonded greased monostrands are common in post-tensioned floor slabs. Fibre-reinforced polymer tendons are studied for coastal structures because they do not rust. Search for external prestressing, unbonded post-tensioned slabs and the history of Freyssinet's early bridges.

The tendon alone leaves 2.5 N/mm² tension at the top and 12.5 N/mm² compression at the bottom; the 56 kN·m load then gives 8 N/mm² at the top and still 2 N/mm² compression at the bottom.
